findings.claim: Practice question 2 reads 'Give two reasons why people commit crimes.', is labelled '1 mark - Give/Name', and its mark scheme says '1 marks for each correct reason, up to 2 marks ... [2 marks]'.
findings.truth: The spec sets one five-part question per theme worth 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12 marks. There is no 2-mark part, so a 1-mark question takes one point. The label and the scheme also contradict each other.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2 Component 2: Thematic studies - 'marks will be allocated as follows; 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12'

findings.claim: Practice question 2 reads 'Name two aims of punishment.', is labelled '1 mark - Give/Name', and its mark scheme awards '[2 marks]'.
findings.truth: Same as F1: no 2-mark part exists in this paper. One mark, one point.

findings.claim: Mark scheme for question 6: Tutu 'believed that "without forgiveness, there is no future", reflecting Jesus's teaching on reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18-19)'.
findings.truth: 2 Corinthians is a letter written by Paul. The ministry-of-reconciliation passage is Paul's teaching, not a saying of Jesus. Attributing a New Testament letter to Jesus is a wrong attribution a student could repeat in an answer.

findings.claim: 'The Bible warns: "The love of money is the root of all kinds of evil" (1 Timothy 6:10).' The same wording is repeated in a knowledge-check stem and a flashcard stem.
findings.truth: The NIV reads 'For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil'. The KJV reads 'the love of money is the root of all evil'. The quoted wording matches neither translation.

findings.claim: Gee Walker 'said: "I can't hate. I have to forgive them. Unforgiveness makes you a victim, and I refuse to be a victim."' A shortened form of the same quotation appears in the question 6 mark scheme.
findings.truth: Her documented words are 'I have to forgive them. I can't feel anger and hatred, because that is what killed my son.' The published sentence is a composite that no source supports, presented in quotation marks and attributed to a living named person.

findings.claim: 'Anthony Walker, a Black British teenager, was murdered in a racially motivated attack in Liverpool.' A knowledge-check stem repeats 'in Liverpool in 2005'.
findings.truth: Anthony Walker was killed with an ice axe in Huyton, in the Metropolitan Borough of Knowsley, Merseyside, on 29-30 July 2005. Huyton is not in Liverpool.

findings.claim: The death penalty 'was abolished in the UK in 1965'.
findings.truth: The Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965 suspended the death penalty for murder in Great Britain for five years; Parliament made it permanent in 1969 (Northern Ireland 1973). It stayed on the statute book for a small number of other offences, such as treason, until 1998. '1965' alone is only true for murder.
findings.evidence: Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965; Crime and Disorder Act 1998

findings.claim: Item 4: 'The aim of punishment that focuses on helping criminals change their behaviour is called _____.' Options are retribution, deterrence, reformation, rehabilitation; 'reformation' is keyed correct.
findings.truth: Rehabilitation is a synonym of reformation in this context, so a student who understands the idea can be marked wrong. The distractor must be a different concept.
findings.evidence: recomputation of the answer key against the options

findings.claim: 'examiners want to see that you understand the complexity of the issue' (lesson 1) and 'examiners want to see that you understand the tension between forgiveness and justice' (lesson 3).
findings.truth: Neither claim can be sourced. House rule forbids invented statements about what examiners reward. The advice itself is sound, so only the examiner framing is removed.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: 'The 12-mark evaluation question often asks you to weigh these two principles against each other.'
findings.truth: An unevidenced claim about how often a question is set. 'May ask' is accurate.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated exam claims

findings.claim: 'Both agree that forgiveness leads to reconciliation and is ultimately better for the individual and society.'
findings.truth: The same lesson says some Christians separate forgiveness from reconciliation, which 'may not always be possible or safe', and the glossary defines reconciliation as going beyond forgiveness. Forgiveness can open the way to reconciliation; it does not lead to it automatically.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with lesson 3 paragraph n9 and the reconciliation glossary entry

findings.claim: Mark scheme for question 4: 'Islam - the Qur'an supports retribution as a principle of justice: "We ordained for them: a life for a life, an eye for an eye" (5:45).'
findings.truth: Qur'an 5:45 reports a ruling given to the Children of Israel in the Torah. The lesson body states this carefully; the mark scheme drops it and reads as though the verse prescribes retribution for Muslims. The Qur'anic basis for qisas among Muslims is 2:178.
findings.evidence: Qur'an 5:45 and 2:178 (quran.com); lesson 2 content paragraph n3

findings.claim: '...how to balance justice with compassion. the specification identifies four main categories of reasons for crime.'
findings.truth: The sentence starts with a lower-case 'the'.

findings.claim: Every 4-mark and 6-mark mark scheme in all three lessons opens 'Students may include two of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited', and each 12-mark scheme ends '[12 marks] [plus spelling/grammar 3 marks]'.
findings.truth: The opening sentence is AQA's own mark-scheme rubric, which the house copyright rule says never to paste, though it is not on the validator's banned-string list. Options: (a) leave it, since it is not banned and the same sentence runs through every RS unit; (b) restate it in house wording, for example 'Two developed points are needed; any other valid point also earns credit', as a subject-wide sweep rather than a single-unit edit. The SPaG tag is also loose: 3 SPaG marks are awarded once for the paper on performance in the 12-mark questions, not 3 marks per question.

findings.claim: 'Islamic law (Shari'ah) permits the death penalty for certain serious offences, including murder and apostasy.'
findings.truth: Classical Sunni jurisprudence does prescribe death for apostasy, so the statement is not false, but the ruling rests on hadith rather than the Qur'an and many contemporary scholars reject it. Stated flat, it reads as settled law.

findings.claim: Allah is 'the most merciful' (Ar-Rahman) in lesson 1; Ar-Rahman ('the Most Merciful') in lesson 3.
findings.truth: Ar-Rahman is normally rendered 'the Most Gracious' or 'the Most Compassionate'; Ar-Rahim is 'the Most Merciful'. The gloss used here is common in GCSE textbooks, so it will not cost marks.

findings.claim: 'The eighth: "You shall not steal"' and 'The sixth: "You shall not murder"'.
findings.truth: Correct in the Protestant and Jewish numbering, which is the usual GCSE listing. Catholic and Lutheran numbering makes them the seventh and the fifth, and this board sets Catholic Christianity as a separate religion. No edit, because the ordinals given are the ones most students meet.
findings.evidence: Exodus 20; Catechism of the Catholic Church commandment numbering

findings.claim: Lesson 3 is titled 'Forgiveness & Corporal Punishment' but contains no corporal punishment content at all; corporal punishment is covered in lesson 2.
findings.truth: The title promises material the lesson does not hold. Title is not an editable field in this pass, so it is recorded only.

summary: Three lessons, 18 findings, 19 edits. The scripture, the case studies and the answer keys are mostly sound; the real damage is two impossible 2-mark practice questions, a New Testament letter attributed to Jesus, a composite quotation put in Gee Walker's mouth, and the wrong town for the Anthony Walker murder. Smaller fixes cover a misquoted 1 Timothy 6:10, the 1965 death-penalty date, a knowledge check whose distractor is a synonym of the keyed answer, and three invented examiner claims.
